opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Waymo is one of those cases where you can see a transformative technology arriving, and I think there are a few reasons to be excited.

The first is the most direct: safety. Over a million people die on the world's roads every year, and tens of thousands in the US alone. Most of those crashes come down to human error: distraction, fatigue, intoxication, speeding. The data Waymo has been publishing suggests their vehicles are involved in substantially fewer injury-causing crashes than human drivers over comparable miles. If that holds up as they scale, it's an enormous amount of suffering avoided. It's rare to see a technology where the humanitarian upside is that concrete and measurable.

The second is what it does for people's lives. Think about people who can't drive: older people, people with disabilities, kids, people who can't afford a car. Reliable autonomous transport could give them a kind of freedom and independence they don't have now. And for everyone else, it gives back time. Commuting becomes time you can read, rest, or talk with someone.

The third reason is more about what it signals, and this connects to my broader interest in AI governance. Self-driving is one of the first places where we're deploying a highly capable AI system in a safety-critical, physical, public setting. Society is working out, in real time, how to evaluate it, how to set standards, how to share data with regulators, how to assign liability, and how to build public trust. Waymo's approach has been relatively cautious: lots of testing, gradual expansion city by city, and fairly transparent safety reporting. I think that's a useful template. It shows you can move toward deployment while taking safety seriously, and that safety and commercial success don't have to be in tension.

Finally, there's the experience of it. When people ride in one for the first time, there's this moment of nervousness, then within a few minutes it feels completely normal. That's a nice microcosm of how quickly we adapt to powerful technology. It's exciting, and also a reminder that we should think carefully, ahead of time, about the norms and institutions we want in place before more capable AI systems become just as ordinary.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety, access, commuting time, and AI governance, but does not identify reducing car manufacturing for mostly idle vehicles.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reclaiming urban parking space for other uses.

fable-5.1.text:
Allan Dafoe: Honestly, a lot of it is just that it works. I remember the first time I got in one in San Francisco and had this slightly uncanny feeling of watching the steering wheel turn on its own, and then within about three minutes I'd stopped noticing. It felt like a very ordinary cab ride, except calmer. That's a remarkable thing for a technology to pull off, that it becomes boring so quickly.

But I think the reason it excites me goes beyond the gadget. For years self-driving cars were the canonical example people pointed to when they wanted to say AI was overhyped. The timelines kept slipping, the demos didn't generalise, and there was this long tail of weird situations that seemed to defeat the whole approach. And now there's a deployment where, if you look at the safety data, it appears to be meaningfully safer than human drivers on the same roads. So it's a concrete example of a hard real-world problem that sat in the "almost there" state for a long time and then actually got solved.

The other piece I find interesting is how it was done. Waymo went slowly and carefully, city by city, with a lot of testing, a lot of engagement with regulators, a lot of willingness to be embarrassed by their own caution while competitors moved faster and made bigger claims. And that cautious path seems to be the one that's winning. That's a hopeful data point for how transformative technologies can be rolled out: that you can be deliberate about safety and still arrive at something people genuinely want to use.

And then there's the welfare angle, which I don't want to lose. Over a million people die on roads every year worldwide. If this scales, that's one of the clearest examples of AI delivering an enormous, measurable reduction in human suffering. When I think about what we want the broader story of AI to look like, that's close to it: real capability, deployed responsibly, with the benefits spread widely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety, deployment, and reduced road deaths, but does not mention reducing car manufacturing or idle vehicles.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reclaiming urban parking space or putting it to other uses.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the prospect of taking something that’s both incredibly useful and quite dangerous — driving — and making it much safer. We’re used to the risks of human driving, so they can fade into the background. But if we can build systems that reliably do better, that would be a tremendous benefit.

There’s also the independence it could give people who can’t drive. And I find it exciting as a concrete example of AI working in the physical world: dealing with messy situations and interacting with people. Of course, the safety case needs to be demonstrated. But the possibility of safer, more accessible transportation is pretty compelling.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safer driving and accessibility, but does not identify reducing car manufacturing because cars sit idle as a benefit.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reclaiming urban parking space or using it more productively.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the possibility of taking a technology that still feels a bit like science fiction and making it genuinely useful in everyday life. You get into a car, there’s no one in the driver’s seat, and it takes you where you want to go. That’s pretty remarkable.

But the bigger promise is safety. Driving is something we do routinely that carries substantial risk. If autonomous cars can become reliably safer than human drivers, that could be an enormous benefit. And they could give much more independence to people who can’t drive.

I also find it interesting as an example of how to deploy AI: in a bounded setting, with a lot of testing, and expanding as you gain evidence that it works. That doesn’t solve the challenges of more general AI, but it gives us something concrete to learn from.
